parts.title: Joining a bike-share scheme
parts.context: A man phones to register for a city bike-share scheme.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning to join a city bike-share scheme. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: City Bikes, Lucy speaking. How can I help you?

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Hi, I'd like to sign up for the bike scheme. I was thinking of the annual membership, but I'm only here until the summer, so I'll go for monthly.

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: OK, monthly membership. I'll register you now.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The man chooses monthly membership, so 'monthly' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: Can I take your full name?

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Raj Desai. The surname is D-E-S-A-I.

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: Thank you. And your address?

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Flat six, Barton House, on Mill Lane.

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: Barton House. Got it. And I need your date of birth, please.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: The nineteenth of August, nineteen ninety-eight.

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: Thanks. We ask everyone what they'll mainly use the bikes for. It helps us decide where to put new stations.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Well, I work from home, so not for work. Mainly to get to college. I do evening classes in the city centre three times a week.

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: College. And just out of interest, how did you hear about us?

script.speaker: raj
script.text: A friend of mine uses the bikes, but I'd never thought about it until I heard an advert on the radio last week.

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: The radio. That's good to know, it's a new campaign.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: So how much is the monthly membership?

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: It's normally fifteen pounds a month, but we've got a launch offer at the moment, so for you it's twelve.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Great. And is there a charge each time I use a bike?

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: The first thirty minutes of every ride are free. After that it's fifty pence for each extra half hour.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: That's fine, most of my journeys are about twenty minutes. What if I leave the bike somewhere else, outside the college, say?

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: You must always return it to a station. If you leave it anywhere else, there's an extra charge of twenty pounds, because we have to send someone to collect it.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Understood. And if something's wrong with a bike, a flat tyre for example?

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: Every bike has a red button on the handlebars. Press it, and it reports the problem automatically, and that bike won't be given to anyone else until it's fixed.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Clever. So when can I start?

script.speaker: lucy
script.text: We'll post you a membership card. It should arrive within five working days. Until then, you can use the code I'll send you by text.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Perfect. Thanks very much.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: The new Central Library
parts.context: The head librarian talks about a city library that has reopened after building work.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear the head librarian talking about the reopening of a city library. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.

script.speaker: owens
script.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to the reopening of Central Library. I'm David Owens, the head librarian. As many of you know, the library has been closed for eighteen months. People often assumed we were just redecorating, but the real reason was that asbestos was found in the ceilings, and it had to be removed safely before anyone could use the building again. While we were closed, we took the opportunity to repair the roof as well.

script.speaker: owens
script.text: There are a few changes to how borrowing works. You can still take out up to twelve books at a time, as before, and the self-service machines are where they've always been, by the entrance. What's new is that the loan period is now four weeks instead of three, so you'll have more time to finish that long novel.

script.speaker: owens
script.text: And here's some news I think you'll like: from today, there are no more fines for returning books late, for anyone, adults included. Many libraries have found that fines simply put people off coming back, especially families.

script.speaker: owens
script.text: You'll also notice that we now have a café. It isn't run by the council or by one of the big chains. It's run by a local charity that trains young people who are looking for work, so every coffee you buy helps someone get a job.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.

script.speaker: owens
script.text: Let me explain where everything is now, because quite a lot has moved. The children's library used to be upstairs, but parents told us that carrying buggies up the stairs was a nightmare. So it's now on the ground floor, next to the café.

script.speaker: owens
script.text: The quiet study room is at the very top of the building, on the second floor, as far as possible from the noise of the children and the café. It has forty desks, and you can book them online.

script.speaker: owens
script.text: The public computers are on the first floor. There are twice as many as before, and staff are there to help if you need it.

script.speaker: owens
script.text: The local history archive has stayed exactly where it was, on the first floor, so regular researchers won't have to learn a new route. You'll need to show your library card to go in.

script.speaker: owens
script.text: One thing I'm especially excited about is our new recording studio, where anyone can record music or a podcast. It's on the second floor, and it's fully soundproofed, so it won't disturb the study room next door.

script.speaker: owens
script.text: And finally, there's a new exhibition space on the ground floor, just inside the entrance. The first exhibition is of photographs of the city from the nineteen fifties. Do have a look on your way out.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A river fieldwork report
parts.context: Two geography students discuss the method and results of their river fieldwork.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two geography students, Nadia and Tom, discussing the report on their river fieldwork. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: OK, Tom, let's get the method section finished. I think we should describe exactly what we did at each of the five sites, in order.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: Fine. So the first thing we did at every site, before anyone stepped in the water, was take photographs of the river banks, so we could compare the shape of the channel.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Right. Then we stretched a tape measure from one bank to the other to measure the width.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: And after that, we used the metre stick to record the depth every fifty centimetres across the river. That took the longest.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Then the speed of the water. We timed a float over ten metres, three times, and took the average.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: We used an orange, didn't we? It floats just under the surface, so the wind doesn't affect it much. And finally, we picked up ten stones from the riverbed at random and measured how long each one was.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: That's it. We didn't take any water samples in the end, so we'll leave those out.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: We should also mention the problem at site three.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Yes, the fallen tree. The water was fine, and we didn't have any trouble with cows like at site one, but a tree had come down right across the river, so we had to move the site about fifty metres downstream.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: Now, the results. Most of it matched the theory. The river got wider and deeper as we went downstream, and faster too.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Except for the stones. They should get smaller downstream, but at site four they were much bigger than at site three.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: I don't think we measured them wrongly, and there hadn't been a flood. I think it's the old quarry just above site four. Stones from the quarry must be washing into the river there.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: That makes sense. What should we do about site two, where we lost the depth measurements?

script.speaker: tom
script.text: We could estimate them, but that's not very scientific, and we can't go back because the course finishes next week. I think we should just explain what happened and leave that site out of the depth results.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Agreed. And how should we show the speed of the river?

script.speaker: tom
script.text: A table's a bit dull, and a bar chart doesn't really show the change as you go downstream. A line graph would show the trend best.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Good. And one last thing. I've reread the whole report, and I think the weakest part is the conclusion. It just repeats the results. It needs to link back to the theory we started with.

script.speaker: tom
script.text: You're right. I'll rewrite it tonight.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the history of paper money
parts.context: An economics lecture on how paper money began and how it has changed.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history of paper money. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon. Today we're going to look at something most of us carry every day without a second thought: paper money. Its story begins in China, more than a thousand years ago.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: At that time, Chinese coins were made of iron or bronze, and they had holes in the middle so they could be carried on strings. The trouble was that they were extremely heavy. A merchant travelling to buy goods might need thousands of them.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So merchants began leaving their coins with a trusted merchant in one city and receiving a paper receipt, which they could exchange for coins in another city. These receipts were known as flying money, because they moved so easily.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In the eleventh century, the government took control of printing these notes, mainly to prevent forgery, which had become a serious problem. It was the first true paper currency. But the government soon discovered how tempting it was to pay its bills simply by printing more notes, and the result was inflation: prices rose so fast that the notes became almost worthless.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Europeans were astonished when they first heard about paper money. Marco Polo described how the emperor's notes were made from the inner bark of mulberry trees, and how people accepted them as if they were gold.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: It took several more centuries for banknotes to appear in Europe. The first were issued in Sweden, in sixteen sixty-one. The reason was rather unusual. Sweden's coins were made of copper, and since copper is worth much less than silver, the coins had to be enormous. Some weighed nearly twenty kilos, so paper was a welcome alternative.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: From the start, banknotes were a target for criminals, and the history of money is also a history of security features. Early notes used watermarks and complicated designs, and later, special ink that changes colour when the note is tilted.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The biggest recent change is the material. Australia introduced notes made of polymer, a kind of plastic, in nineteen eighty-eight, and many countries have since followed. Polymer notes last much longer than paper ones, and they're far harder to copy, which has reduced forgery dramatically.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: And what of the future? Cash is used less every year, and many central banks are now testing digital currencies, which would exist only electronically. Whether paper money will disappear completely, however, is a question we'll come back to next week.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
